title: Given a Scenario, Apply Network Security Features, Defense Techniques, and Solutions

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: After identifying risks and attacks, administrators apply controls that reduce exposure and restrict unauthorized access.
bullets: Device hardening, disabling unused ports/services, and changing default passwords
NAC, port security, 802.1X, and MAC filtering
ACLs, URL filtering, and content filtering

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given a network-security scenario, choose whether to reduce the attack surface, control who connects, protect cryptographic keys, filter traffic or content, or isolate systems into appropriate zones.
bullets: Turn off unnecessary interfaces/functions → Disable unused ports and services
Replace factory credentials → Change default passwords
Restrict a switch port → Port security
Allow/deny a MAC address → MAC filtering

sections.title: Device Hardening
paragraphs: Device hardening removes unnecessary exposure so systems are more difficult to attack.

entries.title: Disable Unused Ports and Services
paragraphs: Every unused switch interface, management protocol, and application service adds attack surface. If it is not needed, disable it.
entries.memoryHook: Turn off what you do not need.

entries.title: Change Default Passwords
paragraphs: Factory credentials are widely known and routinely targeted. Replace them before deploying a device.
entries.memoryHook: The factory password is an attacker's first guess.

sections.title: Network Access Control

entries.title: Network Access Control (NAC)
paragraphs: NAC is a broad framework that determines whether a user or device may join the network, potentially evaluating identity and endpoint status first.

entries.title: Port Security
paragraphs: Port security restricts which devices can use a specific switch interface.
entries.memoryHook: This switch port accepts only approved devices.

entries.title: 802.1X
paragraphs: 802.1X provides authentication-based, port-level network access control for wired or wireless connections.

entries.title: MAC Filtering
paragraphs: MAC filtering permits or denies listed hardware addresses. Because a MAC address can be spoofed, it is weak identity proof by itself.
entries.memoryHook: Is this MAC address on the list?

sections.callout: Broad admission framework → NAC. Port authentication → 802.1X. Switch-interface restriction → Port security. Address list → MAC filtering.

sections.title: Key Management
paragraphs: Key management protects the complete cryptographic-key lifecycle: creation, storage, distribution, rotation, and revocation. Poor key handling can defeat otherwise strong encryption.

sections.title: Security Rules and Filtering

entries.title: Access Control List (ACL)
paragraphs: An ACL permits or denies network traffic using criteria such as source, destination, protocol, and port.
entries.memoryHook: Traffic matches a rule, then allow or block.

entries.title: URL Filtering
paragraphs: URL filtering controls access to web destinations by URL or category.

entries.title: Content Filtering
paragraphs: Content filtering evaluates the material or file type itself and blocks prohibited, unsafe, or unwanted content.

sections.callout: Network traffic criteria → ACL. Web destination → URL filter. Material itself → Content filter.

sections.title: Trusted, Untrusted, and Screened Zones

entries.title: Trusted Zone
paragraphs: A trusted zone contains controlled internal systems given a higher level of trust.

entries.title: Untrusted Zone
paragraphs: An untrusted zone contains networks that receive no automatic trust; the Internet is the classic example.

entries.title: Screened Subnet
paragraphs: A screened subnet is an isolated buffer network for public-facing web servers, mail gateways, or other exposed services between untrusted networks and the trusted LAN.

sections.callout: Internal → Trusted. External → Untrusted. Isolated middle zone → Screened subnet.

sections.title: Defense in Depth
paragraphs: Security controls are stronger together. A layered design can disable unused ports, replace default credentials, require 802.1X, enforce ACLs, filter web traffic and content, and isolate public servers in a screened subnet.

entries.title: NAC vs. 802.1X
paragraphs: Broad access-control solution → NAC. Specific port-authentication standard → 802.1X.

entries.title: Port Security vs. MAC Filtering
paragraphs: Control switch-port access → Port security. Permit or deny listed MAC addresses → MAC filtering.

entries.title: MAC Filtering vs. 802.1X
paragraphs: MAC address check → MAC filtering. Identity authentication → 802.1X.

entries.title: ACL vs. URL Filtering
paragraphs: Network traffic rule → ACL. Web destination rule → URL filtering.

entries.title: URL Filtering vs. Content Filtering
paragraphs: Where the user goes → URL filtering. What material is transferred → Content filtering.

entries.title: Trusted vs. Untrusted
paragraphs: Internal/higher trust → Trusted. External/low trust → Untrusted.

entries.title: Screened Subnet vs. Trusted Network
paragraphs: Externally reachable isolated systems → Screened subnet. Internal protected systems → Trusted zone.

entries.title: Encryption vs. Key Management
paragraphs: Protect data cryptographically → Encryption. Protect the key lifecycle → Key management.

entries.title: Hardening vs. NAC
paragraphs: Reduce exposure on a device → Hardening. Decide whether an endpoint joins the network → NAC.
